Empirical Research Plan: “Do Households Respond to Marginal or Average Electricity Prices?”

=====================================================================
1. Identification Strategy
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen method: Instrumental‐Variables (2SLS) panel demand estimation with household and time fixed effects.

Why IV?  
•  Endogeneity: under increasing–block tariffs, the marginal (and therefore the average) price is mechanically determined by the household’s own consumption; OLS would bias price elasticities toward zero (simultaneity) and conflate both price concepts.  
•  Exogenous source of variation: California regulators periodically change the entire tariff schedule. Conditional on consumption tiers (kWh blocks) these rate changes shift marginal prices while leaving the location of consumption kinks unchanged. Such changes are not targeted to individual households and are plausibly orthogonal to household‐specific demand shocks.  
•  The tariff schedule is known one month in advance, making predicted prices based on lagged consumption a valid “expected price” instrument à la Ito (2014) and Wichman (2017).

Core idea: use “schedule‐driven” prices that depend only on (i) the regulatory tariff and (ii) predetermined consumption information to instrument the contemporaneous marginal and average prices.

---------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment Variable  
•  T_it ≡ ln(P_it^M)   (log marginal price faced by household i in month t)  
•  We will also run a parallel specification with T_it ≡ ln(P_it^A) (log average price).

Instrument(s)  
Z1_it ≡ ln( P̂_it^M )  Predicted marginal price computed by applying the current month’s tariff to household i’s consumption in the *same* month of the previous year (or 12-month lag).  
Z2_it ≡ ln( P̂_it^A )  Analogous predicted average price.

Control (counterfactual)  
Because every household receives some price, the counterfactual is the value of consumption when the (instrumented) price is at an alternative level. In 2SLS the control comes from households whose tariff‐driven price movements differ in magnitude due to their location relative to block thresholds.

Timing  
Tariff change dates are determined by the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC). These occur 3–5 times in the 1999–2007 window. Instruments vary both at those event months and continuously through differential placement in blocks.

---------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
---------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance – Tariff revisions and lagged‐consumption bins generate substantial within-household variation in predicted price: Cov(Z_it , P_it) ≠ 0.  
• Plausible: tariff changes often exceed 5–10 %, and households are distributed across all blocks.

A2. Exclusion – Conditional on household FE, month×year FE, weather, and demographics, Z_it affects current kWh only through its effect on the actual price, not directly.  
• Plausible: tariff design is exogenous to idiosyncratic demand shocks; last year’s consumption is predetermined.

A3. Independence – Tariff changes are not timed to unobserved demand shocks.  
• Regulatory changes respond to statewide policy/costs, not individual usage.

A4. Monotonicity – When the tariff schedule raises prices in a block, the induced change in P_it is non-negative for all households in that block.  
• Satisfied by design.

A5. SUTVA – One household’s tariff-driven price does not directly affect another’s consumption, conditional on common time effects.  
• Reasonable for electricity.

---------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
---------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Serial correlation between lagged and current consumption shocks  
→ Use weather controls, household FE, and cluster standard errors at the household level. Show that instruments remain strong after adding lagged weather shocks.

T2. Anticipatory behavior (households learn about forthcoming tariff increases)  
→ Instruments use *realized* tariff each month, not announcements. Include month×year FEs so only deviations across blocks identify elasticities.

T3. Differential non-price programs (e.g., energy efficiency subsidies) coincide with tariff changes  
→ Control for enrollment in such programs if recorded; add interaction of time FE × utility district; perform robustness dropping months with major DSM interventions.

---------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
---------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Libraries
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast FE and IV regressions
library(lmtest)      # coeftest, waldtest
library(sandwich)    # vcovCL for clustering

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
d  <- fread("ca_power_1999_2007.csv")   # assume tidy format

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
d[, date         := as.Date(paste(year, month, "01", sep = "-")) ]
d[, ln_kwh       := log(kwh + 1)]           # add 1 to avoid log(0)
d[, ln_p_marg    := log(price_marg)]
d[, ln_p_avg     := log(price_avg)]

# Instrument: predicted prices using last year’s usage ----------------
setorder(d, household_id, date)
d[, kwh_lag12    := shift(kwh, 12), by = household_id]

# Function to compute bill & prices for a kWh level given tariff
get_prices <- function(kwh_vec, tariff_id, tariff_table){
  # tariff_table must list: tariff_id, block_upper, block_price
  # returns list(marg_price, avg_price)
  res <- mapply(function(q, id){
    tf <- tariff_table[tariff_id == id]
    # cumulative blocks
    tf[, block_kwh := pmin(block_upper, q) - shift(c(0, block_upper[-.N]), fill=0)]
    bill <- sum(tf$block_kwh * tf$block_price)
    list(marg = tf$block_price[which.max(tf$block_upper >= q)],
         avg  = bill / q)
  }, kwh_vec, tariff_id, SIMPLIFY = FALSE)
  res_marg <- sapply(res, `[[`, "marg")
  res_avg  <- sapply(res, `[[`, "avg")
  return(list(marg = res_marg, avg = res_avg))
}

# assume tariff_table already loaded
tmp <- get_prices(kwh_vec = d$kwh_lag12,
                  tariff_id = d$tariff_id,
                  tariff_table = tariff_table)
d[, ln_p_marg_hat := log(tmp$marg)]
d[, ln_p_avg_hat  := log(tmp$avg)]

# Weather controls  ---------------------------------------------------
d[, `:=`(tmean = (tmax + tmin)/2,
         hdd   = pmax(65 - tmean, 0),
         cdd   = pmax(tmean - 65, 0)) ]

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main IV regressions
# Elasticity wrt marginal price
iv_marg <- feols(ln_kwh ~ 1 | ln_p_marg ~ ln_p_marg_hat | 
                 household_id + ym(date) + hdd + cdd,
                 data = d, cluster = ~household_id)
summary(iv_marg)

# Elasticity wrt average price
iv_avg  <- feols(ln_kwh ~ 1 | ln_p_avg  ~ ln_p_avg_hat  | 
                 household_id + ym(date) + hdd + cdd,
                 data = d, cluster = ~household_id)
summary(iv_avg)

# Horse race: include both prices simultaneously (each instrumented)
iv_both <- feols(ln_kwh ~ 1 | 
                 c(ln_p_marg, ln_p_avg)  ~ c(ln_p_marg_hat, ln_p_avg_hat) |
                 household_id + ym(date) + hdd + cdd,
                 data = d, cluster = ~household_id)
summary(iv_both)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness: Alt. instrument using tariff change dummies only
d[, tariff_change := as.integer(date %in% tariff_change_dates)]
iv_alt <- feols(ln_kwh ~ 1 | ln_p_marg ~ tariff_change |
                household_id + ym(date) + hdd + cdd,
                data = d, cluster = ~household_id)
summary(iv_alt)
```

---------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory: under rational “marginal” decision‐making, demand responds primarily to the contemporaneous marginal price, not the average bill.  
•  We expect a negative elasticity with respect to marginal price: ε_M ≈ −0.2 to −0.4 (in line with short-run residential electricity estimates).  
•  After controlling for marginal price, the coefficient on average price should be close to zero. If instead consumers use average cost heuristics, ε_A will be negative and ε_M will shrink.

---------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
---------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument relevance (F-stat > 10) ………………… 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction plausible ……………………. 0.8 (score 1=fully satisfied, 0.8≈“mostly”)  
C3: Independence from shocks ………………………… 0.8  
C4: Monotonicity/no defiers …………………………… 1  
C5: SUTVA/no interference …………………………… 1  

Average score ≈ 0.92 → overall design judged credible, but we will transparently report first-stage diagnostics and conduct placebo tests (e.g., using pre-tariff change months) to bolster C2 and C3.
